t: Largest Subarray Length K — Only the First Element Matters
o: Two same-length arrays compare lexicographically: the verdict is settled at the first index where they differ. Every length-k window of `nums` is a candidate, and because all values are distinct, no two windows can ever tie. In Example 1 (`nums = [1,4,5,2,3]`, `k = 3`) the windows are [1,4,5], [4,5,2] and [5,2,3]; their first elements 1, 4 and 5 already decide everything, so [5,2,3] wins. Example 2 (`k = 4`) compares [1,4,5,2] against [4,5,2,3] — again the first element decides — and Example 3 (`k = 1`) degenerates to finding the global maximum, [5]. With n up to $10^5$, comparing every candidate element-by-element costs O(n·k) in the worst case, but noticing that first elements alone settle the comparison collapses the task to a single O(n) scan for the largest value among indices 0..n-k.
k: All values are distinct, so any two candidate windows differ at index 0 — the whole lexicographic contest is decided by the first element alone.
Therefore the answer is simply the window whose start index in [0, n−k] holds the maximum value.
With duplicates this shortcut dies: equal first elements force real element-by-element checks.

a.i: Enumerate every window of length k and keep the lexicographically largest one seen so far, exactly as the definition prescribes. This works with or without distinct values and is the natural first solution to state aloud. Its cost is proportional to how deep comparisons go, up to k positions per candidate.
s: Initialize the best window as the first one, nums[0..k).
For each start i from 1 to n−k, form the window starting at i.
Compare it lexicographically against the best window and replace the best when larger.
a.t: O(n · k) — each of the n−k+1 candidates may be compared element by element

a.n: Approach 2: Pick the Best First Element
a.i: Distinct values guarantee that two windows never share a first element, so whichever candidate starts with the larger value wins immediately, regardless of what follows. Hence scanning starts 0..n−k for the maximum identifies the answer's start in one pass. This turns an O(n·k) comparison problem into a plain maximum search.
s: Scan start indices i from 0 to n−k.
Track the index whose value nums[i] is maximal.
Return the slice of length k beginning at that index.
a.t: O(n) — a single scan over the n−k+1 legal start indices

w: Go straight to the one-pass maximum scan — after stating the brute force, the "first element decides" argument takes one sentence and interviewers love it. Pitfalls: letting start indices run past n−k (the window must fit inside the array), and forgetting that correctness leans entirely on the distinctness guarantee. Edge cases: k = n (answer is the whole array) and k = 1 (global maximum). The built-in follow-up — duplicates allowed — breaks the shortcut; then either fall back to explicit lexicographic comparison (O(nk) worst case) or discuss smarter schemes such as hashing window contents or suffix-rank comparisons. A related generalization worth mentioning: building the lexicographically largest subsequence of any length with a monotonic stack.
